item.research_question: Can machine learning reliably predict the crystal structure (FCC, BCC, FCC+BCC, MIP) of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) synthesized via melting and casting routes without using synthetic data augmentation, and is synthetic data augmentation a reliable practice for this domain?
item.material_system: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) comprising 30 elements (Al, Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Cu, Mn, Ti, V, Nb, Mo, Zr, Hf, Ta, W, C, Mg, Zn, Si, Re, N, Li, Sn, Be, B, Ag, Pt, Y, Pd, Au); specifically a novel alloy Ni25Cu18.75Fe25Co25Al6.25.
item.processing_route: Vacuum arc melting of elemental buttons (Ni, Cu, Fe, Co, Al; purity > 99.99%) under high purity Ar environment, followed by multiple melting/solidification cycles for homogeneity, vacuum sealing in quartz tube, homogenization at 1000 °C for 10 h, and water quenching.
item.test_conditions: Machine learning models trained on 1200 experimental datasets from melting/casting routes; tested on 240 samples from original data and 279 samples from augmented data (1200 original + 192 synthetic); XRD analysis performed with Cu Kα radiation (λ = 1.54056 Å) at 20°–100° (2θ).
key_findings: The vanilla Random Forest Classifier (V-RFC) achieved the highest performance with an average test accuracy of 84%, ROC-AUC score of 0.9649, and tenfold cross-validation mean score of 0.9315.

Synthetic data augmentation using SMOTE-Tomek links increased average test accuracy to 92% (1392 datasets) but did not yield significant breakthroughs in correct/incorrect phase predictions compared to the original dataset.
The V-RFC model correctly predicted the FCC phase for the newly synthesized alloy Ni25Cu18.75Fe25Co25Al6.25, which was confirmed by XRD showing Bragg's peaks (111), (200), (220), (311), and (222).
Five physical parameters (VEC, ∆χ, ∆Smix, δ, ∆Hmix) were identified as crucial for phase prediction, with no strong multicollinearity observed between them.
The model was limited in interpreting the exact number and types of phases in complex multiphase HEAs, often classifying them broadly as MIP (Mixture of Intermetallic Phases).
Hyper-parameter tuning of the RFC model (HT-RFC) resulted in an approximate 3% increment in average test accuracy to 87.49%.
The study found that mixing data from different synthesis routes causes spurious effects, justifying the exclusion of non-melting/casting routes from the dataset.
item.mechanism: The authors argue that the Random Forest Classifier's ensemble of decision trees effectively handles the imbalanced dataset of experimental data without the need for synthetic augmentation, which they claim introduces uncertainty regarding whether generated samples are truly high-entropy alloys. The model relies on the correlation of five thermodynamic and geometric parameters (VEC, ∆χ, ∆Smix, δ, ∆Hmix) to distinguish between solid-solution phases (FCC, BCC) and intermetallic mixtures (MIP).
item.limitations: The method is limited in exactly interpreting the number and types of phases present in a complex multiphase HEA, as it typically predicts such cases as a single 'MIP' category rather than resolving specific phase combinations.
item.future_work: A follow-on work will test and predict the mechanical properties of HEAs, which will require atomistic studies using Molecular Dynamics (MD) simulations with EAM potentials for 16 elements (Cu, Ag, Au, Ni, Pd, Pt, Al, Pb, Fe, Mo, Ta, W, Mg, Co, Ti, Zr).
quotes: We found that (i) RFC model predictions were more reliable in contrast to other models and (ii) the synthetic data augmentation is not a neat practice in materials science specially to develop HEAs, where it cannot assure phase information reliably.
Based on our RFC model, we report the development of a new HEA (Ni25Cu18.75Fe25Co25Al6.25) exhibiting an FCC phase proving the robustness of our predictions.

Although the ST-RFC model showed a higher average test accuracy of 92%, no significant breakthroughs were observed, when testing the number of correct and incorrect predictions using confusion matrix and ROC-AUC scores for individual phases.
